thread.document:
Hi everyone!

The diffusion lectures introduced a lot of dense math: forward processes, reverse processes, score functions, DDPM vs DDIM, etc. I found it hard to develop intuition for what's actually happening geometrically, so I built an interactive visualization tool using Claude to help understand these concepts.

 Link to Interactive Tool

Click the link above to access the tool directly in Claude. You can interact with all the visualizations yourself!

What This Tool Does

The visualizer helps you understand diffusion models through interactive 2D demonstrations:

1. Forward Process Visualization

Watch data points diffuse from structured distributions (moons, spirals, clusters) into Gaussian noise

Scrub through timesteps with a slider to see how signal and noise trade off

See the exact values of √ᾱₜ (signal) and √(1-ᾱₜ) (noise) at each step

2. Reverse Process Visualization

See how following the score function brings noisy points back to the data manifold

Includes Bayes rule visualization showing why the reverse conditional is Gaussian

Understand why we can start from pure noise and end up with structured samples

3. Score Function Visualization

View the score field ∇ₓ log p(x) as a vector field

See how the score changes from sharp/detailed (low noise) to smooth/uniform (high noise)

Includes density heatmap showing p(x) alongside the score vectors

4. DDPM vs DDIM Comparison

See multiple sampling trajectories side-by-side

DDPM: stochastic trajectories that diverge from the same starting noise

DDIM: deterministic trajectories that always produce the same output

Resample to see how randomness affects DDPM but not DDIM

5. Interactive Image Noise Demo

Apply the forward process to simple images (gradient, checkerboard, circle, face)

Watch structure dissolve as t increases

Reference strip showing key timesteps side-by-side

6. Interactive Manifold Diagram

Drag a "noisy sample" point around high-dimensional space

See the score vector pointing toward the natural image manifold

Animate the denoising process following the score back to valid images

7. Velocity Field Visualization

See the "gas analogy": particles flowing along streamlines

Connects to the probability flow ODE perspective

8. Comprehensive Quiz Bank (50+ questions)

Context-aware quizzes that change based on which tab you're viewing

Questions derived from the diffusion paper covered in lecture

Covers forward process, reverse process, score functions, and DDPM vs DDIM

Detailed explanations for each answer

Track your score and review all explanations

How to Use This for Studying

Start with the Forward Process tab: pick different distributions and watch how they diffuse. Notice how structure persists longer for some shapes than others.



Toggle on the Score Field: see how arrows point toward data at low noise but become uniform at high noise. This is the "coarse-to-fine" intuition.



Switch to Reverse Process: start from t=T and watch points flow back to the manifold. Check out the Bayes rule visualization to understand why the reverse process is Gaussian.



Try the DDPM vs DDIM tab: resample multiple times and notice how DDPM gives different outputs while DDIM is deterministic.



Play with the Image Demo: this connects the 2D toy examples to real image generation.



Drag points in the Manifold diagram: build intuition for how the score always points "toward real images."



Test yourself with the quizzes: each tab has 15-20 questions ranging from basic definitions to deeper conceptual understanding. The explanations are helpful even if you get the answer right!



The Prompt Engineering Process

I worked with Claude Opus 4.5 to iteratively design this tool. Interestingly, I used Claude itself to help me create the prompt. I started by describing what I wanted (interactive diffusion visualizations with geometric intuition), and through back-and-forth conversation, Claude helped me refine the specifications into a detailed prompt. I then used that prompt in a fresh chat to generate the final tool.

After sending the prompt to the new chat, I continued refining the visualization through several iterations:

Made the Score Function tab distinct: Initially the Forward Process and Score Function tabs looked identical; I asked Claude to make the Score Function tab show a density heatmap with prominent score vectors instead of data points

Made the manifold diagram interactive: The static manifold illustration became a draggable demo where you can move a "noisy sample" point and watch the score vector update, then animate the denoising trajectory

Added DDPM vs DDIM comparison: I provided the diffusion paper and asked Claude to add visualizations explaining the math, which led to the side-by-side trajectory comparison showing stochastic vs deterministic sampling

Added Bayes rule and velocity field visualizations: These help explain why the reverse process is Gaussian and connect to the "gas analogy" from the paper

Made the image noise demo interactive: Added a slider to control the noise level and a play/pause animation

Reorganized the layout: I attempted to move the image demo and manifold sections to the top of the right panel so the intuitive examples are immediately visible alongside the main visualizer, but this is not shown in the visualization 

The model failed here

Added the quiz section: Started with regeneratable random questions, then switched to showing all questions at once

Expanded and curated quiz questions: Added more technical questions based on the paper, then removed advanced topics (classifier-free guidance, v-prediction, consistency distillation, etc.) that weren't covered in the paper or lecture

An issue here was that the paper was no longer in the uploads for the chat, and I couldn’t upload it without reaching the length limit. Therefore I think Claude ended up using mostly its own knowledge here.

The key insights for the prompt:

Start with educational goals: what specific confusions should this address?

Specify the math precisely: include the actual equations (β schedule, ᾱₜ, forward/reverse formulas)

Request multiple linked visualizations: 2D toy distributions, actual images, and conceptual diagrams reinforce each other

Ask for interactivity: sliders, toggles, and draggable elements let you explore parameter space

Include dynamic explanations: text that changes based on the current timestep helps connect visuals to concepts

Provide source material: I gave Claude the diffusion paper we're covering in lecture, which helped generate accurate quiz questions and mathematical explanations

Add self-assessment: quiz questions with detailed explanations help solidify understanding

Iterate and curate: Review generated content against source material to remove anything beyond scope

The full prompt I used is provided at the end.

Critical Annotations

Here's my honest assessment of the tool:

What works well:

The forward/reverse process visualizations clearly show the signal/noise tradeoff

Score field visualization makes the "pointing toward data" intuition concrete

DDPM vs DDIM comparison is very effective: you can immediately see the stochasticity difference

The interactive manifold diagram is great for building intuition about high-dimensional geometry

Stats display (√ᾱₜ, √(1-ᾱₜ)) keeps you grounded in the actual math

The quiz questions are well-calibrated and the explanations are helpful

Velocity field visualization connects nicely to the probability flow ODE / flow matching perspective

Potential issues / limitations:

The score field is approximated using kernel density estimation, not a learned neural network. This is pedagogically useful but not exactly what happens in practice

The 2D visualizations are toy examples; real diffusion operates in ~200,000 dimensions for images, where geometry behaves very differently

The "image" demo uses a tiny 12×12 grid, which oversimplifies the complexity of real image diffusion

The Bayes rule visualization uses a simplified 1D example; the actual derivation involves more careful analysis of the Gaussian conditionals

Trajectory simulations use simplified dynamics, real DDPM/DDIM have more nuanced update rules

Generally, Claude Opus 4.5 struggled a lot more with creating this tool than I expected

The final result is good, but it took more chats than I thought it would

Important note about the quiz questions:

The only material I gave the model to generate the quiz questions, besides what it already knew about diffusion, was the paper we were building off of in class

This means some questions may use slightly different notation or framing than what was presented in class

Some questions may cover details from the paper that weren't emphasized in lecture

Use these questions to deepen your understanding of the paper's perspective, but cross-reference with lecture notes and the homework for exam-specific material

Minor technical notes:

The DDPM/DDIM trajectory simulation uses a simplified score-based update rather than the exact DDPM/DDIM formulas, but the qualitative behavior (stochastic vs deterministic) is correct

The velocity field shows E[x₀|xₜ] - xₜ direction, which is related to but not exactly the probability flow ODE velocity

Questions for Discussion

After playing with the tool, consider:

Why does the score field become more uniform as noise increases? What does this mean for early vs. late denoising steps?



In the DDPM vs DDIM comparison, both methods use the same learned score function. Why does adding noise during sampling (DDPM) lead to diversity while removing it (DDIM) leads to determinism?



The manifold diagram suggests the score "points toward real images." But in 200,000 dimensions, what does "toward" even mean? How does the network learn this direction?



The quiz questions are based on the diffusion paper. Did you notice any differences in notation or framing compared to how concepts were presented in lecture?



Hope this helps with studying! The quiz section has 50+ questions across all four topics, so there's plenty to work through. Let me know if you have questions or find any errors in the explanations.

I've added in the prompt, annotated prompt generation chat, and the annotated visualization creation chat below. Hopefully this method could be used to generate visualizations for other concepts as well!
